sentences.text: This petition under Section 166 MV Act is filed by the Petitioner seeking compensation of Rs.25,00,000/- for the injuries sustained by him in a road traffic accident.

2. It is the specific contention of the petitioner that on 05-06-2023 at about 7.45 p.m., he was riding his two-wheeler motorcycle bearing registration number KA-05-EP-0302 from Chalamasandra village towards Shivanahalli village, near Chalamasandra village, Huliyurdurga hobli, Kunigal Taluk,
Tumkur District.
At that time, the driver of an auto-rickshaw bearing registration number KA-06-AA-8520 came in a rash and negligent manner and dashed against the petitioner's two-wheeler.
As a result of the impact, the petitioner fell down and sustained grievous injuries.
He was immediately shifted to Madduru Medical Centre, Madduru, where he was treated as an inpatient and underwent surgery.

3. The petitioner incurred an amount exceeding Rs. 1,00,000/- towards medical expenses,
conveyance, nourishment, and attendant charges.
Before the accident, the petitioner was healthy and earning Rs. 20,000/- per month by working as a labourer, and owing to the injuries sustained

,
he is now suffering from permanent disability, resulting in substantial loss of earning capacity and future income.
The accident occurred solely due to the rash and negligent driving by the driver of the offending vehicle.
Therefore, the petitioner prays that this Tribunal be pleased to award just and proper compensation against Respondents No. 1 and 2, being the owner and insurer of the said vehicle.
4. In response to the petition, Respondents No. 1 and 2 appeared before this Court through their counsel.
But respondent No.1 has not filed the objections.

5. Respondent No. 2, the Insurance Company, has filed its written statement wherein it has denied all the averments made in the petition, though it has admitted the issuance of a valid insurance policy as on the date of the accident.
However, it contends that its liability is subject to the terms and conditions mentioned in the policy.

6. It is specifically contended that the owner of the offending vehicle and the police authorities failed to comply with the mandatory provisions of Section 134(c) of the Motor Vehicles Act and Section 158(6) of the Act, and hence the petition is not maintainable.

It is denied that the offending vehicle was involved in the accident and further contended that the driver of the said vehicle did not possess a valid and effective driving licence as on the date of the accident, thereby absolving the insurer from liability.
It is also contended that the offending vehicle did not possess a valid permit to ply.
7. It is further contended that the accident did not occur due to the negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle but rather due to the negligence of the petitioner himself.
The nature and extent of injuries, treatment, income of the petitioner, alleged disability, and expenses incurred are all denied.
It is also contended that the compensation claimed is highly excessive and exaggerated.

Hence,
Respondent No. 2 has prayed for dismissal of the petition.

8. On the basis of the above pleadings, the following Issues were framed :-

sentences.text:
Whether the Petitioner proves that on 05-06-2023 at about 07-45 p.m., on Chalamasandra-Shivanahalli road, near Chalamasandra village, Huliyurudurga Hobli, Kunigal Tq, Tumkuru District, he sustained injuries in a road traffic accident,
while he was moving on his motorcycle bearing number KA-05-EP- 0302 due to the rash and negligent driving of the driver of the autorikshaw bearing number KA- 06-AA-8520?
2. Whether the respondent No.2 proves that there is violation of the policy conditions by respondent No.1 and respondent No.2 is not liable to pay any compensation?
3. Whether the petitioner is entitled for compensation as claimed?
4. What order or award ?

9. In order to prove the claim, the Petitioner examined himself as PW.1 and in support of his case,
doctor is examined as PW-2 and got marked the documents as per Ex.P.1 to P.14.

On the other hand,
the Respondent No.2 has examined the RTO Inspector, Tumkur as RW-1 and got marked Ex.R.1 to 4 and the official of insurance company is examined as RW-2.
10.

By considering the available materials on record and the arguments addressed by the parties, I have answered the above Issues as under:
Issue No.1: In the Affirmative. Issue No.2: In the Affirmative Issue No.2: Partly in Affirmative.

Issue No.3: As per the final order, for the following:
REASONS 11. ISSUE NO.1: Case of the petitioner that on 05-06-2023 at about 7.45 p.m., he was riding his two- wheeler motorcycle bearing registration number KA- 05-EP-0302 from Chalamasandra village towards Shivanahalli village, near Chalamasandra village,
Huliyurdurga hobli, Kunigal Taluk, Tumkur District.
At that time, the driver of an auto-rickshaw bearing registration number KA-06-AA-8520 came in a rash and negligent manner and dashed against the petitioner's two-wheeler.
As a result of the impact, the petitioner fell down and sustained grievous injuries.
He was immediately shifted to Madduru Medical Centre, Madduru, where he was treated as an inpatient and underwent surgery.
12. In order to substantiate his case, the petitioner entered the witness box as PW.1 filed an affidavit in lieu of examination in chief Under 18 rule 4 of CPC.

He has reiterated the averments of the petition and has produced police documents marked at Ex.P1 to P8, namely, FIR, complaint, spot mahazar, spot sketch, vehicle seizure mahazar, IMV report, wound certificate, and charge sheet.
To further support his claim, Dr. Ramesh B., Orthopedic Surgeon, was examined as PW.2 and produced documents at Ex.P13 and Ex.P14.
As per Ex.P7 - Wound Certificate

sentences.text: The respondent No. 2-Insurance Company, however, raised a specific plea that the accident did not occur due to rash and negligent driving of the autorickshaw, but solely due to the negligence of the petitioner himself.

It is their further contention that the autorickshaw was not at all involved in the accident and that the petitioner, in collusion with the owner of the autorickshaw, set up a false case and lodged the complaint belatedly, after one day of the incident.
During the cross-examination of PW.1, suggestions were put to him regarding his own negligence, false implication of the autorickshaw, and collusive lodging of the complaint after one day.
These suggestions were specifically denied by the petitioner.

14. On careful consideration of the material available on record, this Tribunal finds that except for the bare contention of collusion and delayed complaint, no cogent evidence has been adduced by respondent No. 2 to substantiate its allegations.

Mere delay of one day in lodging the complaint,
particularly when the petitioner was immediately shifted to the hospital for treatment of grievous injuries, cannot be treated as fatal to the petitioner's case.
Such delay is both natural and satisfactorily explained.
15. Further, respondent No. 2 has not chosen to examine either the owner of the autorickshaw or any independent witnesses to establish that the vehicle was not involved in the accident.
No contra evidence has been brought on record to dislodge the version of the petitioner.

On the other hand, the petitioner's version stands corroborated by contemporaneous police records such as FIR, mahazar,
spot sketch, and charge sheet, all of which consistently attribute negligence to the driver of the offending autorickshaw.
16. It is well settled that in motor accident claim cases, the standard of proof is not that of a criminal trial requiring proof beyond reasonable doubt, but that of preponderance of probabilities.
Applying this principle, the plea of collusion raised by the insurer remains a mere allegation without substantiation, whereas the petitioner's evidence is supported by official records.

17. Accordingly, this Tribunal holds that the defence of respondent No. 2 that the accident occurred due to negligence of the petitioner and that the autorickshaw was falsely implicated in collusion cannot be accepted.
The accident is proved to have occurred due to the rash and negligent driving of the offending autorickshaw, resulting in grievous injuries to the petitioner.
Hence, Issue No.1 is answered in the Affirmative.
18. Issue No.2:

Respondent No. 2 has contended that the owner of the offending vehicle violated the terms and conditions of the insurance policy, in as much as the vehicle was not authorized to ply on the road where the accident occurred.
It is specifically alleged that the offending vehicle did not have a valid route permit to operate on the stretch of road at the place of accident.

On this ground,
respondent No. 2 has claimed that it is not liable to indemnify the owner and, therefore, stands absolved of liability to pay compensation to the petitioner.

sentences.text: To substantiate this contention, the RTO, Tumkur, was examined as RW.1.

He produced the vehicle history report at Ex.R4 and the permit at Ex.R3, and deposed that the permit allowed the offending vehicle to operate within the jurisdiction of Huliyurdurga, but not at the place of accident.
In his cross-examination, RW.1 reiterated that no permission was taken by the owner to operate the vehicle at the incident place.
RW.2 further confirmed that the vehicle was plying at the accident spot without a valid route permit, thereby amounting to breach of policy conditions.
Thus, the testimony of RW.1 and RW.2 supports the defence of respondent No. 2 that the offending vehicle was operating outside its authorized route at the relevant time.

20. Reliance was placed on the judgment of the Hon'ble High Court of Karnataka in MFA No.967/2017, Sri Venkatesh v. IFFCO Tokio General Insurance Co. Ltd. & Ors., dated 22.04.2022 and (2018)8, SCC 492, Rani and others Vs. National Ins.Co.Ltd., wherein it was held that when a vehicle had no permit to ply at the accident spot, the Tribunal was justified in exonerating the insurer and directing the owner to satisfy the award.

sentences.text: In the present case, a charge sheet has also been filed against the owner of the offending vehicle for the offence punishable under Section 192-A of the Motor Vehicles Act, alleging that the vehicle was operating without permit in ChamlaSandra village.
On perusal of Ex.R3, it is evident that, as on the date of the accident, the vehicle was covered by a valid permit, but restricted to a specific route.
The record clearly establishes that the accident occurred at ChamlaSandra village, a place not covered under the said permit.
Neither the owner nor the driver of the vehicle has contested the proceedings or produced any rebuttal evidence to show that the vehicle was authorized to ply at the accident spot.

22. Therefore, in the absence of rebuttal, and in light of the oral and documentary evidence adduced by respondent No. 2, it stands established that the offending vehicle was being operated outside its authorized route.
Hence, I answer issue no.2 in the Affirmative.

23. ISSUE NO.3:-As per Ex.P7 - wound certificate, the Petitioner sustained crush injuries, mid-foot dislocation, multiple fractures of the right foot, and open grade III-B wound, which are opined as grievous in nature.

The medical records and treatment papers further confirm that the Petitioner was admitted as an inpatient and underwent surgical procedures including wound debridement,
K-wire fixation of the metatarsal bone, and closed reduction with fixation for mid-foot dislocation.
Subsequently, the Petitioner underwent removal of K-wire and continued to experience pain and difficulty in carrying out routine activities.

24. To substantiate the nature of disability, PW2 - Dr. Ramesh, Orthopedic Surgeon, deposed that upon clinical and radiological evaluation, the Petitioner was found to have non-union of the first metatarsal bone with residual dislocation.

5 assessed the permanent disability of the right lower limb at 24% and of the whole body at 12%.
25.

However, during the course of cross- examination, PW2 candidly admitted that he had not personally treated the Petitioner at the time of hospitalization, but had examined him subsequently for assessment.

Furthermore, PW2 did not furnish any specific opinion on the functional disability,
i.e., how far the physical disability translates into actual impairment of earning capacity and performance of day-to-day activities.
The assessment made by PW2 is therefore on the medical/physical basis only, and not on occupational functionality.

It is now a settled principle of law that while medical evidence is important, the Tribunal must independently consider the functional impact of the disability, especially keeping in view the nature of the vocation of the injured.

In the present case, it is undisputed that the Petitioner was working as a mason/labourer,
which is a profession requiring prolonged standing, balancing, climbing, and strenuous use of the lower limbs.
Even a partial permanent disability of the right foot would have a significant bearing on the Petitioner's earning capacity in such a manual profession.

That considering the site and seriousness of the injuries, the medical evidence of 24% disability to the right lower limb, the admitted absence of specific findings on functional impairment, and the occupational requirements of the Petitioner, this Tribunal is of the view that the whole-body disability cannot be mechanically adopted at 12% as assessed by PW2.
Instead, for the purposes of assessing loss of future earning capacity, a functional disability of 7% to the whole body is more appropriate.
This assessment balances both aspects the medical evidence of significant permanent damage to the right foot, and the lack of direct clinical opinion on functional earning incapacity.

26. Thus, the Tribunal holds that the Petitioner has sustained a functional disability of 7% to the whole body, which shall be applied while computing compensation under the head of loss of future earning capacity.
27. In the petition, the age of the petitioner is mentioned as 48 years.
As per Exhibit P9 - Aadhaar Card, his year of birth is shown as 1975.
Accordingly, his age as on the date of the accident is considered as 48 years.

Therefore, the appropriate multiplier applicable to the case at hand is '13'.
28.
At the time of the accident, the petitioner was doing labour work and claimed to be earning a sum of Rs. 20,000/- per month.
Due to the injuries sustained in the accident, he has suffered permanent disability, resulting in loss of earning capacity and future income.
29. However, the petitioner has not produced any documentary evidence to substantiate his occupation or income.
In the absence of proof of income, this Tribunal deems it appropriate to assess the income based on the notional income guidelines issued by the Karnataka State Legal Services Authority

As the accident occurred in the year 2023, the notional income is taken as Rs.
16,000/- per month for the purpose of computation of compensation.

30. Thus this tribunal is of the opinion that the petitioner who sustained the injuries is entitled for compensation under the following heads:

Loss of future income on account of permanent disability:
Considering the petitioner's grievous injury which has resulted in performing daily vocational activities, this court is of the opinion that the functional disability of 7% is reasonable and just.
32. The petitioner was 36 years old as on date of alleged accident and the multiplier applicable to the petitioner as per decision laid down by Hon'ble Apex court in Sarla Verma's case is at 15.
The notional income taken as Rs.16,000 x 12 x 13 x 7/100= Rs.1,74,720/- towards loss of future income.
33. Pain and sufferings:

So far as the compensation under non-pecuniary damages are concerned,
considering the nature of the grievous injury, which has resulted in performing daily vocational activities, as well as the duration of inpatient treatment and physical and mental suffering endured by the petitioner, this tribunal is of the opinion that an amount of .30,000/- would be just and fair compensation under head of Pain and sufferings 34. Loss of amenities of life: undoubtedly the petitioner is suffering from difficulties in performing day to day activities and is facing continuous hardship due to the disability.
Therefore this tribunal finds to appropriate to award a sum .25,000/- under head of loss of amenities of life.
35. Medical expenses:
Under the pecuniary damages, expenses relating to treatment, hospitalization and medicines, the Petitioner has produced medical bills at Ex.P.12 amounting to Rs.64,654/-.
There is no evidence forthcoming to disbelieve the said medical bills.
On perusal of medical bills, it appears that the petitioner has spent Rs.64,654 /- towards medical treatment.
The medical bills appears to be genuine.
Therefore, the Petitioner is awarded compensation of .64,654/- towards Medical Expenses.
36. Conveyance, food, nourishment and attendant charges: Ex.
P.10 -Discharge
summary shows that Petitioner was admitted at Maddur Medical Centre, Maddur as an inpatient from 05-06-2023 to 10-06-2023 i.e., totally for a period of 6 days.
Therefore, it is just and reasonable to award compensation of .10,000/- under the head of conveyance, food, nourishment and attendant charges.
37. Loss of earning during laid up period:

With regard to the loss of earnings during treatment period, Considering the nature of the grievous injury, which has resulted in significant difficulty in carrying out daily vocational activities, as well as the duration of impatient treatment and recovery,
this tribunal considers the 2 months for rest is considered .

As the monthly income of the Petitioner is already considered as .16,000/- per month, loss of earning during laid up period would be .16,000 x 2 = Rs.32,000/-.
38.

Thus the compensation awarded under the various heads are as under:

Liability:

It is the specific defence of respondent No. 2 - the insurance company - that the owner of the offending vehicle violated the terms and conditions of the policy, inasmuch as the vehicle did not possess a valid route permit at the time of the accident.

The documentary evidence, namely Ex.R4 - Vehicle History Report and Ex.R3 - Permit supports this contention, as it clearly establishes that the vehicle was not covered by a valid permit for the route on the date of accident.

Undoubtedly,
the absence of a valid permit constitutes a breach of the policy condition by the insured.

40. However, it is a well-settled principle of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh & Ors., (2004) 3 SCC 297, that such a breach does not absolve the insurer from its statutory liability to indemnify third- party victims of motor vehicle accidents.

entities.text: National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh & Ors., (2004) 3 SCC 297
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The liability of the insurer under Section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, being statutory in nature, cannot be defeated by internal breaches of contract between the insurer and the insured.

41. Therefore, this Tribunal is of the considered view that mere omission of sub-section (4) of section 149 does not take away either the statutory liability of the insurer to satisfy third-party claims in the first instance, or the insurer's right to recover such amount from the insured in cases of breach of policy conditions.

42. Thus, even though respondent No. 2 has established that the owner of the offending vehicle committed a breach by permitting the vehicle to ply without a valid route permit, this defence cannot defeat the lawful claim of the petitioner.
Respondent No. 2, being the insurer, is directed to satisfy the award in the first instance and pay the compensation to the petitioner along with interest at 6% per annum.
Thereafter, respondent No. 2 shall be entitled to recover the said amount from respondent No. 1 - the owner of the offending vehicle - in accordance with law.
I have answered Issue No.3 partly in the Affirmative.
43. ISSUE NO.4 :

In view of the above discussion, reasons stated and findings given to Issue Nos. 1 to 3, I proceed to pass the following:

which is a profession requiring prolonged standing, balancing, climbing, and strenuous use of the lower limbs.
Even a partial permanent disability of the right foot would have a significant bearing on the Petitioner's earning capacity in such a manual profession.
That considering the site and seriousness of the injuries, the medical evidence of 24% disability to the right lower limb, the admitted absence of specific findings on functional impairment, and the occupational requirements of the Petitioner, this Tribunal is of the view that the whole-body disability cannot be mechanically adopted at 12% as assessed by PW2.
Undoubtedly,
the absence of a valid permit constitutes a breach of the policy condition by the insured.
40. However, it is a well-settled principle of law laid down by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh & Ors., (2004) 3 SCC 297, that such a breach does not absolve the insurer from its statutory liability to indemnify third- party victims of motor vehicle accidents.
The liability of the insurer under Section 149 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, being statutory in nature, cannot be defeated by internal breaches of contract between the insurer and the insured.
41. Therefore, this Tribunal is of the considered view that mere omission of sub-section (4) of section 149 does not take away either the statutory liability of the insurer to satisfy third-party claims in the first instance, or the insurer's right to recover such amount from the insured in cases of breach of policy conditions.
42. Thus, even though respondent No. 2 has established that the owner of the offending vehicle committed a breach by permitting the vehicle to ply without a valid route permit, this defence cannot defeat the lawful claim of the petitioner.
opennyai_summary.arguments: The accident is proved to have occurred due to the rash and negligent driving of the offending autorickshaw, resulting in grievous injuries to the petitioner.
opennyai_summary.decision:
Therefore this tribunal finds to appropriate to award a sum .25,000/- under head of loss of amenities of life.
Respondent No. 2, being the insurer, is directed to satisfy the award in the first instance and pay the compensation to the petitioner along with interest at 6% per annum.
Thereafter, respondent No. 2 shall be entitled to recover the said amount from respondent No. 1 - the owner of the offending vehicle - in accordance with law.
I have answered Issue No.3 partly in the Affirmative.
43. ISSUE NO.4 :
In view of the above discussion, reasons stated and findings given to Issue Nos. 1 to 3, I proceed to pass the following:

8 ORDER
Claim Petition filed under Sec.166 of M.V.Act is allowed in part with cost.
Petitioner is awarded compensation of Rs.3,36,374/- together with interest @ 6% p.a.
from the date of petition till the date of deposit with the Tribunal.
Respondent No.1 is liable to pay the compensation as awarded by this Tribunal.
Respondent No.2 - Insurance  company shall deposit aforesaid  amount within two months from the date of this order and recover the entire compensation amount along with interest from the Respondent No.1 in view of violation of terms of insurance policy.
After deposit of the compensation amount, 25% of the amount shall be kept in FD in the name of petitioner in any nationalized or scheduled bank of his choice for a period of 2 years.
Remaining 75% amount shall be disbursed to the petitioner through E- payment on proper identification.
Advocate's fee is fixed at .1,000/-.
Draw award accordingly.
